content.text: Where a modal sits changes the meaning. ¬◇P says P is impossible. ◇¬P says only that P might be false.
□(P → Q) says the whole if then holds in every world. P → □Q says that if P is true, Q is necessary.

content.definition: Two claims could both be true together: ◇(A ∧ B).
A entails B when B must be true if A is: □(A → B).

examples.title: Impossible, or possibly not
lines: It isn't possible that you're careful: ¬◇C
It's possible that you're not careful: ◇¬C
examples.note: The first rules out every world where you are careful. The second needs only one world where you are not.

examples.title: The whole, or a part
lines: Necessarily, if you're a dentist, you're tough: □(D → T)
If you're a dentist, you're necessarily tough: D → □T
examples.note: The second says a dentist could not have been anything but tough.

examples.title: Someone, necessarily
lines: It's necessary that someone is strong: □∃x S(x)
examples.note: In the first, the strong one may differ from world to world. In the second, one person is strong in every world.

question.prompt: Which formula says 'It isn't necessary that N is true'?
question.hint: Is the 'not' in front of 'necessary', or in front of 'N is true'?
question.explanation: 'It isn't necessary that N' denies □N, so it is ¬□N. N may still be true, just not in every world.
